text: Madurai Shanmukhavadivu Subbulakshmi (16 September 1916 – 11 December 2004) was a renowned Indian Carnatic singer. She was the first musician to receive the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour, and the first Indian musician to be awarded the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 1974. She was also the first Indian to perform at the United Nations General Assembly in 1966. Born on 16 September 1916 in Madurai, Madras Presidency, she was the daughter of veena player Shanmukhavadivu Ammal and Subramania Iyer, with her grandmother Akkammal being a violinist. Her mother, from the devadasi community, was a music exponent and regular stage performer, and Subbulakshmi grew up in a highly musical environment. Her musical development was influenced by interactions with Karaikudi Sambasiva Iyer, Mazhavarayanendal Subbarama Bhagavathar, and Ariyakudi Ramanuja Iyengar. She began learning Carnatic music under her mother and later studied Hindustani music under Pandit Narayanrao Vyas. Her first public performance was in 1927 at the age of eleven in the 100-pillar hall of the Rockfort Temple, Tiruchirappalli, with Mysore Chowdiah on violin and Dakshinamurthy Pillai on mridangam, organized by F. G. Natesa Iyer. In 1929, at age 13, she performed bhajans at the prestigious Madras Music Academy, a traditionally male-dominated institution that broke its norms by inviting a young girl as a key performer; her performance was described as spellbinding and earned her the moniker of musical genius, establishing her as one of the leading Carnatic vocalists. By age seventeen, she was giving concerts independently, including major performances at the Madras Music Academy. She toured internationally as India's cultural ambassador, performing at the Edinburgh International Festival of Music and Drama in 1963, Carnegie Hall in New York, the UN General Assembly on UN Day in 1966, the Royal Albert Hall in London in 1982, and the Festival of India in Moscow in 1987. In 1969, she performed at Rameswaram with Indian Railways Advisor SN Venkata Rao, singing in front of each idol in the Ramanathaswamy Temple, and maintained a cordial relationship with Sree Ramaseva Mandali in Bengaluru, performing 36 concerts there. After the death of her husband Kalki Sadasivam in 1997, she retired from public performances, with her last concert occurring in 1997. She passed away on 11 December 2004 at her home in Kotturpuram, Chennai. Subbulakshmi acted in four Tamil films during her youth; her debut film, Sevasadanam, was released on 2 May 1938, opposite F. G. Natesa Iyer, directed by K. Subramanyam, and was a critical and commercial success, praised by Ananda Vikatan as "Go see" and described by veteran Marxist leader N. Sankaraiah as an "unusual film" for addressing marriages between young girls and old men, highlighting the suffering of the girl and the mental agony of the aged husband. Tamil film critic Aranthai Narayanan noted that the film marked a turning point in Tamil cinema by showing the aged husband discarding his sacred thread, a symbolic blow to Brahmin orthodoxy. She also played the male role of Narada in Savitri (1941) to raise funds for her husband's nationalist Tamil weekly, Kalki, and took on the title role of Meera in the 1945 film, which gave her national prominence and was later remade in Hindi in 1947. Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru remarked, "Who am I, a mere Prime Minister before a Queen, a Queen of Music," while Lata Mangeshkar called her Tapaswini, Ustad Bade Ghulam Ali Khan referred to her as Suswaralakshmi, and Kishori Amonkar labeled her the ultimate eighth note or Aathuvaan Sur. Sarojini Naidu called her the "Nightingale of India." Her famous bhajan renditions include Meenakshi Pancharatnam, Bhaja Govindam, Vishnu sahasranama, Hari Tuma Haro, and the Venkateswara Suprabhatam. She received numerous honours, including being named a resident artist Asthana Vidhwan of Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams, and a bronze statue of her was installed by the Tirupati Urban Development Authority in Poornakumbham circle on 28 May 2006, unveiled by Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Y. S. Rajasekhara Reddy. The Kancheepuram saree shade MS Blue was named after her by Sri Muthu Chettiyar. A commemorative postage stamp was issued on 18 December 2005 to mark her birth centenary. She received substantial prize money with most of it donated to charity, having conducted over 200 charity concerts and raised more than Rs. 10,000,000. She was awarded honorary degrees from several universities. She was a devoted follower of Kanchi Mahaswamigal and performed his composition "Maithreem Bhajatha" at the UN in 1966. She made a 20-minute recording of "Venkatesa Suprabhatam" for His Master's Voice, with royalties going to the Veda Patasala run by Tirupati Tirumala Devasthanam, and donated many royalties from her best-selling records to various charity organizations.
